Ostorhinchus doederleini undergoes an initial period of rapid development after hatching, with the yolk-sac larva phase lasting only a few days. Under controlled conditions maintained at 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], hatching occurs after approximately 5 days [ab = approximately 5 days] of incubation. Newly emerged prolarvae are lecithotrophic and entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, with a calculated wet weight at birth of just 0.00038 grams [Wwb = 0.00038 grams], a figure derived from the guessed egg diameter of roughly 0.9 millimeters. This extremely modest initial mass reflects the small, transparent eggs typical of marine pelagic spawners and accelerates yolk depletion and mouth opening under the prevailing thermal regime, which enhances metabolic processes. The transition to first exogenous feeding follows shortly after yolk absorption completion, marking the onset of the planktonic larval phase. During this free-swimming stage, individuals grow rapidly while remaining vulnerable to predation and advection.

The larval metamorphosis of Ostorhinchus doederleini marks a critical developmental bottleneck, involving a complete body plan reorganisation and a shift from a pelagic to a benthic existence. At a stable temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C], this morphological transformation is observed at a standard length of 1.10 centimeters , with the event occurring 22 days after hatching . This relatively brief pelagic larval duration is typical of tropical apogonids and facilitates rapid juvenile recruitment to reef habitats. The allometric shift during metamorphosis involves the ossification of fin rays, the development of scales, and pronounced changes in pigmentation. Post-metamorphic juveniles then settle into crevice-dwelling roles, where they begin to assume the cryptic, nocturnal habits characteristic of the species. During this period, body mass increases substantially: the wet weight at this stage is approximately 0.0124 grams , representing a 30-fold increase over the natal mass and reflecting efficient feeding in the planktonic environment.

Reproductive maturation in Ostorhinchus doederleini proceeds steadily after settlement, with puberty defined by the onset of gonadal recrudescence. Individuals reach a standard length of 4.3 centimeters [Lp = 4.3 centimeters] at puberty, and the corresponding wet weight is 1.39 grams [Wwp = 1.39 grams]. The chronological age at which this developmental milestone is achieved is 70 days after hatching [tp = 70 days after hatching] at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C]. This rapid attainment of sexual maturity relative to the species' ultimate size is a notable life-history trait, enabling early recruitment to the breeding population. The body mass at this stage is more than a thousand times greater than that at birth, indicating a period of sustained, efficient growth. Following maturation, individuals begin to allocate resources toward reproductive effort, engaging in pair-spawning behaviors typical of the genus, all under the species' typical thermal conditions of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].

Adult Ostorhinchus doederleini are iteroparous spawners, and their reproductive output under optimal conditions has been characterized through controlled aquarium observations. Reproductively active females can produce approximately 27 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 27 eggs per spawning event], with individual pairs capable of spawning on a near-daily basis, achieving as many as one spawning event per day [F_R_i = one spawning event per day]. This high frequency translates into a prodigious annual fecundity. The ultimate standard length attained by fully grown adults is 8.6 centimeters [Li = 8.6 centimeters], a value that places the species among the larger members of its genus, and from which the corresponding ultimate wet weight is estimated at 15.3 grams [Wwi = 15.3 grams] through the established length–weight relationship. This final body size is typical for a medium-sized cardinalfish and supports the energetic demands of sustained, frequent spawning over several reproductive seasons.

Life-history theory predicts trade-offs between early reproduction and longevity, and in Ostorhinchus doederleini the maximum lifespan appears to be constrained by the energetic costs of such high fecundity. The maximum recorded lifespan under laboratory conditions at 28.5 °C is 368 days [am = 368 days], a relatively short duration for a reef fish, though it is worth noting that wild Japanese populations are reported to live as long as 7 years (King and Finn 2014, Wiki), suggesting substantial intraspecific plasticity in response to environmental conditions and predation regimes at a temperature of 28.5 °C [T = 28.5 °C].
